strengths: Strong empirical results: First method to surpass FP32 baseline on Transformer quantization (29.71 vs 27.5 BLEU in Table 4), demonstrating genuine practical impact
Clear problem formulation and novel perspective: Perturbation-based modeling of quantization discontinuities offers fresh theoretical angle compared to gradient approximation approaches
Practical simplicity and universality: Closed-form ridge regression solution requires no gradient estimation tricks, clipping, or architecture modifications, enabling training with standard recipes

Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple precision levels (1-4 bits), diverse architectures (ResNet-50, Transformer), extended training experiments, and ablation studies on block size and regularization parameter
Elegant signal decomposition: Clear intuition for how regularization parameter λ controls trade-off between signal preservation and noise suppression (Figure 1b)
Thorough comparison with prior work: Tables 2 and 4 demonstrate competitive or superior results versus multiple baselines, and method comparison includes what operations each baseline requires
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: Propositions 1-2 are trivial limiting cases; no convergence analysis, sample complexity bounds, or formal characterization of when/why the method works better than alternatives

Insufficient analysis of core phenomenon: Tables 3-4 show low-precision models outperforming FP32 baselines, but paper only attributes this to vague 'regularization effects' without principled investigation of when perturbations help vs. hurt

Computational overhead not addressed: Ridge regression and data reshaping add overhead (acknowledged but dismissed); no actual runtime measurements, FLOPs analysis, or hardware efficiency metrics provided, undermining deployment feasibility claims

Weak biophysical motivation: Section 2.2 motivates SNNs but Section 5.1.3 produces standard transformers with 1-bit activations, not true SNNs. Abstract claims about 'bridging artificial and biological networks' are oversold relative to evidence

Underdeveloped hyperparameter guidance: λ=0.01 used uniformly despite Table 8 showing extreme sensitivity (5.83 vs 21.42 BLEU); block size B=128 appears arbitrary despite Table 7 showing smaller blocks significantly improve 1-bit models

Limited sparsification development: Section 4.4 is brief (~200 words); sparsification-toward-mean justified only intuitively; structured sparsity results confined to supplementary material; unclear when to apply sparsification vs. quantization alone
Narrow experimental scope: Only 2 architectures and 2 datasets; claims of 'universality' would be strengthened by vision transformers, RNNs, or other modalities

Reproducibility concerns: Some implementation details unclear (e.g., 'true quantization and match matrix multiplication'); numerical stability issues mentioned but not addressed; no safeguards against NaN values observed in Table 8

strengths: Clear problem formulation addressing the important challenge of ultra-low precision training
Technically sound implementation with practical results demonstrating training at 1-bit precision without immediate divergence
Comprehensive experimental coverage across two architectures (ResNet-50, Transformer) and two domains (vision, NLP)
Well-presented methodology with clear code snippets facilitating reproducibility
Unified framework handling both quantization and sparsification
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines existing techniques (perturbation modeling from prior work [17, 23], standard ridge regression) without fundamental innovation
Weak theoretical contribution: Propositions 1 and 2 are trivial (asymptotic behavior and tautological recovery); no convergence analysis or formal stability guarantees

Hyperparameter sensitivity contradicts core claims: Table 8 shows 3.7× BLEU difference across λ values; Table 7 shows 8.7% performance variance with block size, undermining 'universal' and 'robust' characterizations
Overstated empirical claims: claims 'no clipping' but min-max scaling (Eq. 1) is implicit clipping; claims 'off-the-shelf recipes' despite requiring careful λ and block-size tuning
Unfair baseline comparisons: primarily compares against 2019-2021 methods; dismisses recent approaches (BitNet, AWQ) without head-to-head evaluation using identical training recipes

Critical practical limitations downplayed: (1) 1-bit models show 20.67% accuracy drop (23.64 vs 29.8 BLEU) contradicting 'highly competitive' claims, (2) requires 4× longer training for extreme precision, (3) data reshaping creates performance bottleneck at low precision acknowledged in Section 5.2.2
Missing rigorous ablations: no isolated analysis of ridge regression contribution vs. simple L2 regularization, learning rate scheduling, or other standard regularization schemes
No statistical significance testing, error bars, or multiple runs reported; appears to be single-run results
Weak connection to biological motivation: 20% BLEU drop for binary transformers doesn't support 'biophysically plausible' neural networks claim
Incomplete implementation details: no mention of code release; key details relegated to supplementary material; reproducibility concerns regarding exact hyperparameter selection procedures

strengths: Simple and universal approach requiring no gradient estimation, clipping, calibration, or architectural modifications—a meaningful practical contribution
Strong results at extreme quantization (1-bit weights/activations) where existing methods diverge, with successful training using standard recipes
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple architectures (ResNet-50, Transformer), datasets (ImageNet, WMT2014), and settings with ablations on key hyperparameters
Clean mathematical formulation with closed-form ridge regression solution; intuitive decomposition separating signal from quantization noise
Demonstrates competitive or better-than-baseline performance, particularly A4W4 Transformer surpassing FP32 baseline on WMT
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty: ridge regression application is relatively incremental; modeling quantization as perturbations builds on prior work; lacks deep convergence analysis or justification for why this approach is superior to alternatives

Critical computational overhead not analyzed: no actual training time measurements despite claiming efficiency; ridge regression and sub-channel reshaping add non-trivial overhead especially at low precision where integer arithmetic should dominate

Contradicts 'universal' and 'simple' claims: λ shows dramatic sensitivity (BLEU 5.83→21.42 in Table 8); different precisions require different λ values (0.0001 for ≥4-bit, 0.01 for 1-bit); block size significantly impacts accuracy (Table 7: 29.71→27.14 BLEU)

Marginal improvements at practical precision levels: ResNet-50 A4W4 is only 0.04% better than FP32 baseline (within noise); real gains only at 1-bit where alternatives fail; extended training (4× epochs) required, confounding whether improvements come from the method or longer training
Sparsification results less convincing than quantization: modest improvements at moderate sparsity (Table 6, 50%: +0.53 BLEU); claims of 'significant improvements' are overstated
Limited recent baseline comparisons: most comparisons with 2018-2021 methods; recent methods (AWQ 2023, BitNet 2023) mentioned but not fairly compared; makes assessing relative standing difficult

Hyperparameter and design choice justification gaps: why ridge regression specifically? Why L2 regularization on scaling factor `a`? Min-max scaling simplicity not justified; generalization to other quantization schemes unclear
Reproducibility concerns: no training time measurements; hardware specifications missing; variance across random seeds not discussed; some baseline results estimated from figures

strengths: Clear identification and articulation of STE's fundamental limitation (quantization-oblivious backward pass) through well-motivated problem analysis
Principled approach: dequantization transform derived from ridge regression objective rather than heuristics, with clean closed-form solutions
Elegant unified framework treating both quantization and sparsification as additive error injections with unified dequantization
Novel technical contribution: efficient affine quantized matrix multiplication (Theorem 1) reducing overhead from O(4) terms to standard MM + O(MP) rank-1 corrections
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse scales (nanoGPT to Gemma 4B) and domains (LLM, vision, translation) with extensive ablations
Strong empirical results: enables stable training of previously unstable configurations (A1W1, A1.5W1.5); demonstrates quantized larger models outperform smaller full-precision baselines
Practical methodology: uses standard off-the-shelf recipes without complex hyperparameter tuning across different precisions
Excellent reproducibility: code snippets provided, clear implementation details, comprehensive appendix
weaknesses: Limited theoretical justification for why ridge regression specifically solves STE's problem; connection between forcing error into gradients and ridge regression formulation lacks rigor; no convergence analysis or stability guarantees provided

Regularization parameter λ serves dual critical roles (enabling error-aware gradients AND preventing numerical collapse) but this dependency suggests core mechanism is insufficient; choice λ=0.01 appears arbitrary despite robustness claims

Energy efficiency claims are significantly overstated: metric (Eq. 9) explicitly excludes 'dominant costs of data movement' and quantization overhead; acknowledged as merely a lower bound yet presented as primary efficiency measure throughout paper; no actual hardware validation provided

Experimental limitations: (1) Mini-training setup (25k steps, 6.5B tokens) rather than full pretraining—unclear if gains persist in production; (2) No fair comparisons with concurrent methods implementing affine quantization; (3) Single runs without error bars despite ultra-low precision being inherently sensitive to variance; (4) Some results show significant drops (Table 11: 20%+ for A1W1 transformers)
Hardware implementation gap: Claims about bitwise operations and efficiency remain aspirational; no actual hardware measurements, power/speed validation, or deployment pathway demonstrated
Presentation: critical insights (dual role of λ, energy metric limitations) relegated to appendix; Section 3's three-stage formulation could be clearer upfront; dense main paper limits accessibility

Incomplete technical analysis: computational cost of statistics calculation during training not discussed; sparsity extension's claim that dequantization 'inherently learns to correct combined errors' lacks rigorous justification; sparse model performance drop relative to dense baseline not fully addressed

Missing comparisons: no hardware-measured energy vs. theoretical metric; limited analysis of scaling beyond 4B parameters; biological neural network connection (Section 2.3) feels disconnected from main contributions

strengths: Clear articulation of STE's central problem (quantization-oblivious backward pass); elegant 'ghost of departed quantities' framing
Principled ridge regression-based dequantization with closed-form solutions
Comprehensive experiments across multiple model scales, architectures, and tasks with thorough ablations in appendix
Practical achievement of stable A1W1 training where STE diverges (Figure 1(a), Table 1)
Clever and useful Theorem 1 shortcut formula making affine quantization computationally efficient
Unified treatment of sparsification as quantization is conceptually clean
Well-written paper with clear motivation, good figures, and detailed appendix
weaknesses: Weak theoretical justification for core claims: ridge regression objective's connection to quantization robustness is indirect; error δ remains detached from computation graph; appears to substitute one gradient approximation for another rather than solving the non-differentiability problem
Critical hyperparameter λ primarily prevents numerical instability (division by zero when Var_q=0), not a principled 'denoising knob' as claimed; calls into question theoretical grounding
Missing direct experimental comparisons with concurrent method QuEST (Panferov et al., 2025); limited ParetoQ comparison (only nanoGPT/GPT-2 small); significant omission for top-tier venue
Limited experimental scale: main Gemma results use miniature pre-training (25k steps, 6.5B tokens), not convergence; raises questions about generalization

Suspicious results where quantized models beat full precision (Tables 9-11, e.g., A4W4 BLEU 33.78 > FP32 33.5), suggesting confounding factors (implicit regularization from quantization) or hyperparameter tuning asymmetry

Energy efficiency metric (Eq. 9) acknowledged to omit dominant costs of data movement; Pareto frontiers speculative without actual hardware measurements; 'radically simpler hardware' claims are aspirational not demonstrated

Method complexity contradicts 'simple drop-in' claims: requires selecting linear vs. affine quantization, SCQ block size (128 main but Table 12 shows 32 sometimes better), λ value (0.01 claimed universal but Table 13 shows precision-dependent optimality)
No wall-clock time or real hardware energy measurements provided despite efficiency claims; only theoretical complexity analysis (A.4)
A1W1 binary transformer results (BLEU 28.27, Table 11) competitive but not state-of-the-art; presented as achievement but modest compared to claims
Block size sensitivity not fully explored: Table 12 shows extreme variance (29.71 @ size 32 → 27.14 @ size 512 for A1W1), critical design choice treated as secondary

strengths: Clear identification of STE's fundamental limitation (quantization-oblivious backward pass) with compelling motivation
Principled ridge regression-based dequantization transform with clean closed-form solutions
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple domains (LLMs, vision, translation) and model scales
First to enable stable A1W1 training with standard recipes where STE fails demonstrably
Novel efficient affine quantization shortcut (Theorem 1) reducing four-term expansion to one matmul + two rank-1 corrections
Extensive reproducibility: code snippets, detailed hyperparameters, 25-page appendix with thorough ablations
Practical 'drop-in' solution eliminating need for complex recipe tuning, improving usability versus competitors
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core contribution is applying ridge regression to reconstruction, acknowledged similar prior work (Defossez et al., 2021; Ballé et al., 2016) without clear distinction
Lack of theoretical analysis: no convergence guarantees, optimization bounds, gradient error analysis, or formal justification for why ridge regression is optimal
Hyperparameter λ shows high sensitivity (Table 13: 5.83 vs 21.42 BLEU across λ values) contradicting 'universal' claim of λ=0.01; no principled selection method or adaptive learning
Energy efficiency metric (Eq. 9) explicitly acknowledged as first-order approximation omitting dominant costs of data movement and quantization overhead, undermining efficiency frontier claims
Incomplete pre-training experiments: only 25k steps (6.5B tokens) for Gemma rather than full pre-training, limiting conclusions about real-world effectiveness

Comparison fairness concerns: baselines (BitNet, ParetoQ) use 'publicly available symmetric implementations' lacking affine support; unclear if gains come from method or being first to implement affine variants
Sparsification treatment feels forced (treating as quantization form) with mixed results (1:4 hurts accuracy, 2:4 marginally helps); unclear if benefits are method-specific or just integration
Hardware feasibility largely unaddressed: 1-bit networks require specialized hardware (XNOR, popcount) with limited current support; deployment barriers not discussed
Sub-channel quantization adds hyperparameter requiring tuning (Table 12: performance degrades with smaller blocks), contradicting 'universal' drop-in narrative
Recent method QuEST (Panferov et al., 2025) mentioned but not experimentally compared despite being claimed concurrent work
